summary: Stack policy for deciding when async work, Redis, queues, schedulers, durable workflows, and worker processes are actually needed.
description: A portable stack-decision pack that helps agents choose simple in-process work, cron, queue workers, Redis-backed queues, durable workflow engines, or managed jobs based on real product signals.
plainLanguageSummary: Use this when a project is about to add background jobs, queues, cron, Redis, Inngest-like workflows, workers, or retry-heavy async behavior.
bestFor: Apps adding email sending, imports, exports, webhooks, notifications, billing sync, or AI processing
Brownfield projects where background work already exists but ownership and proof are unclear
Greenfield projects where agents may over-add Redis or queues too early
notFor: A synchronous request that finishes quickly and does not need retry or scheduling
A one-off script where operational runtime is not durable product behavior
A project that already has an accepted local stack decision for the same capability
userQuestions: Does this work need retries, backpressure, scheduling, cancellation, or progress visibility?
Can the task safely run inside the request, or does it need a worker boundary?
Who owns local development, production monitoring, and failure recovery for this async path?
qualityBar: The agent must explain why a queue, Redis, cron, or durable workflow is needed before adding it.
Every new async stack dependency needs local-dev notes, production notes, failure handling, and validation gates.
The simplest reliable option wins; do not add infrastructure because it is fashionable.
agentUse: Load this pack before adding Redis, BullMQ, Inngest, cron jobs, worker processes, durable workflows, or async retries.
Ask a guided stack question when signals are mixed instead of silently choosing infrastructure.
Record the accepted stack decision in project memory before broad implementation.

appliesWhen.summary: The project needs work to run outside the request path or after a user action completes.
evidence: Email, notification, import, export, billing sync, webhook, or AI job
Long-running operation that should not block a web request
Worker, jobs, queue, schedule, cron, or workflow language in code or docs

appliesWhen.summary: The work needs retry, rate limiting, idempotency, backpressure, or failure recovery.
evidence: Third-party API calls can fail or throttle
User-visible work needs retry after process restart
Multiple jobs may arrive faster than they can be processed

appliesWhen.summary: The project needs recurring, scheduled, or delayed work with a clear owner.
evidence: Cleanup, reminder, or report generation schedule

avoidWhen.summary: Do not add queue infrastructure for quick deterministic work that can finish safely in the request.
Do not add a worker or Redis dependency without an owner for local dev, deployment, monitoring, and recovery.
evidence: No monitoring or failure recovery plan

rules.title: Start with the simplest reliable async shape
rules.summary: Use synchronous code, framework-native jobs, or a small scheduled command when the work does not need queue durability, backpressure, or cross-process retry.
rules.rationale: Infrastructure adds real operational cost. Skopos should help agents avoid Redis or queue systems until product signals justify them.
examples: Use a framework task or hosted scheduler for one daily cleanup job
Keep a quick internal status recalculation in the request when it is deterministic and cheap
antiPatterns: Adding Redis because a job might exist later
Creating a queue for a fast local-only operation with no retry need

rules.title: Use a queue when durability and backpressure matter
rules.summary: Choose a queue or durable workflow when work needs retries, process isolation, rate limiting, failure recovery, idempotency, or progress tracking.
rules.rationale: Important async work should not disappear on process restart or overload the request path.
examples: Use a queue for bulk CSV import with retries and progress
Use a durable workflow engine for multi-step billing or onboarding flows
antiPatterns: Firing unrecoverable promises from request handlers
Running third-party retry loops inside UI actions

rules.title: Async stack changes need an operational contract
rules.summary: Any new queue, scheduler, worker, Redis, or durable workflow dependency must document local development, production ownership, failure handling, and validation gates.
rules.rationale: Agents can add infrastructure quickly, but teams live with deployment, monitoring, and recovery costs.
examples: Document worker dev command, retry policy, dead-letter behavior, and production alerting
Record why Inngest, BullMQ, Temporal, a hosted scheduler, or framework jobs were chosen
antiPatterns: Adding a Redis dependency without local setup notes
Shipping worker code with no proof command or failure-mode test
